query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In a single‐phase high‐entropy alloy, service‐relevant thermal or mechanical loading induces localized, nanoscale short‐range ordering (SRO) at the grain boundaries. This localized ordering—absent in the as-cast state—reduces intergranular cohesion and shifts the fracture mode toward brittle, intergranular failure, even though conventional grain-boundary segregation and intermetallic precipitation are suppressed.
generation.material_initial_state: A compositionally complex, single‐phase high‐entropy alloy with a uniform disordered matrix and clean grain boundaries, showing high toughness and ductility.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to controlled thermal aging and/or cyclic mechanical loading that simulates extended service conditions.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted across service-relevant temperature ranges (e.g., moderate temperatures where diffusion is activated) and under controlled mechanical strain rates to provoke stress-assisted ordering, while keeping grain coarsening minimal.
generation.structural_mediator: The development of nanoscale short‐range order (SRO) or composition fluctuations at the grain boundaries, acting as a localized structural modifier.
generation.mechanism: Under thermal or mechanical driving forces, local compositional fluctuations become energetically favorable at the grain boundaries, triggering SRO. This induced ordering impairs grain-boundary cohesion and inhibits dislocation transmission across boundaries, leading to a marked reduction in toughness despite the absence of conventional intermetallic phases.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline state, the treated samples will exhibit measurable SRO features localized at grain boundaries (observable via atom probe tomography or high-resolution TEM), a shift in fracture mode from ductile (dimpled rupture) to intergranular cleavage, and a significant drop in fracture toughness.
generation.baseline: The as-cast, single-phase high-entropy alloy with uniform grain boundaries, exhibiting high toughness and ductility with no detectable SRO or secondary phase segregation.
generation.boundary: The effect is anticipated under service conditions where the thermal energy or mechanical stress is sufficient to induce localized SRO at grain boundaries. Outside these conditions (e.g., very low temperatures with negligible atomic mobility or extremely high temperatures where complete disorder returns), the mechanism may not be active.
generation.uncertainty: It remains uncertain how small fluctuations in composition or residual stresses might confound the observation of such SRO, and whether alternative mechanisms (e.g., suppressed but eventual nano-precipitation) might contribute to the embrittlement under similar conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy specimens: one set remains at the as-cast baseline while the other is subjected to a controlled thermal aging or cyclic loading treatment. Characterize the grain boundaries using atom probe tomography and high-resolution TEM to quantify any emergence of short-range order. Simultaneously, measure fracture toughness and analyze fracture surfaces to detect a transition from ductile to intergranular failure.
measurements: Quantification of nanoscale SRO at grain boundaries via atom probe tomography or HRTEM with FFT analysis.
Fracture toughness tests comparing treated versus baseline samples.
Fractographic analysis (e.g., SEM) to determine the fracture mode (dimpled vs. intergranular cleavage).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated specimens do not exhibit an increase in grain-boundary SRO or local compositional ordering, yet still show reduced toughness and a change in fracture mode, or if classical segregation or intermetallic precipitates are observed as the dominant feature, then the hypothesis that SRO is the primary mediator of embrittlement in this HEA would be falsified.
